newsitem.title: HONG KONG: CLP expects "satisfactory" year results.
newsitem.headline: CLP expects "satisfactory" year results.

text.p: China Light & Power Co Ltd said on Friday it expected satisfactory recurrent profits in the year to September 30, 1997.
China Light on Friday reported that interim earnings to March 31 rose to HK$2.64 billion, up 7.3 percent from HK$2.46 billion in the previous corresponding period.
"It is anticipated that the overall growth rate of recurrent earnings for the year ending September 30, 1997 will be satisfactory," the company said in a statement.
China Light said turnover rose to HK$8.90 billion, compared to HK$7.75 billion in the previous first half.

Earnings per share rose to HK$1.26, up only 2.4 percent compared to the previous corresponding period because of the dilution effect of the issue of new shares to CITIC Pacific Ltd during the half year, it said.
China Light generates and supplies electricity to Kowloon and the New Territories in Hong Kong, and also sells some surplus power to the southern China grid.
However, it said manufacturing sales fell by 5.7 percent, reflecting the migration of the territory's industrial sector.
HSBC James Capel analyst Tim Ramsbottom had forecast net profits of HK$2.73 billion, and said he would probably revise down his forecast of HK$5.64 billion for the full year to September 30.
The Estimate Directory consensus forecast tips a HK$5.941 billion full-year profit.
Amsteel Securities' Marvin Lo said he had expected 8.6 percent profit growth, predicting HK$2.67 billion interim profits for the six months to March 31.
Amsteel Securities has forecast HK$6.10 billion full year earnings for the company, which has been under recent scrutiny because of expected falls in capital expenditure.
China Light said on Monday that it had agreed to defer units seven and eight of its Black Point power station for up to five years following a slowdown in growth in electriciy demand.
The government and CLP will review the situation in 1999.
The utility's earnings growth is tied to the growth in its fixed assets under a Scheme of Control (SOC) worked out between the company and the government.
Building more capacity lifts profits, while reducing capital expenditure reduces future earnings.
